title: Cloud Computing: Renting Computers by the Minute

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of NIST's five essential characteristics of cloud computing?
questions.rationale: Clouds use RESOURCE POOLING - multi-tenant hardware shared among customers. Dedicated hardware per customer is private-cloud territory, the opposite of pooling. Self-service, elasticity and metered billing are all core NIST traits.

questions.question: In which service model does the provider manage everything except your data and application configuration?
questions.rationale: SaaS delivers the finished application (Gmail, Salesforce): you only supply data and settings. IaaS stops at virtualised hardware, PaaS adds the runtime platform, and FaaS runs code fragments per event.

questions.question: A developer wants to deploy a web app without managing servers, OS patches or runtime updates - just push code. The best fit is:
questions.rationale: PaaS (Heroku, App Engine, Vercel) exists precisely for push-code-and-go deployment. IaaS hands you a VM and leaves the OS to you; colocation rents rack space for machines you own.

questions.question: The main difference between containers and virtual machines is that containers:
options: Share the host kernel and virtualise only userland
Run a full guest operating system each
questions.rationale: Containers package an app with its libraries above a SHARED kernel - hence megabyte images and second-scale starts. VMs virtualise hardware and each carries a full guest OS, giving stronger isolation at gigabyte cost and minute-scale boots.

questions.question: A hospital keeps patient records on its own dedicated infrastructure but bursts analytics jobs to a public provider. This is a:
questions.rationale: Hybrid combines private infrastructure (sensitive workloads, compliance) with public capacity for spiky overflow. Pure private never leaves the organisation; pure public would host everything on shared provider hardware.

questions.question: Adding more identical servers behind a load balancer is called:
questions.rationale: Horizontal (scale out) multiplies machines; vertical (scale up) buys a bigger single box. The cloud's elasticity machinery is built on horizontal patterns, since instances can be added and removed automatically.

questions.question: Kubernetes is best described as:
questions.rationale: Kubernetes schedules containers across clusters, restarting failed pods, scaling them and rolling out updates. Hypervisors virtualise hardware for VMs; Kubernetes sits a layer above, managing container fleets.

questions.question: In 'serverless' computing, the term is misleading because:
options: Servers still exist - the provider manages them and you never provision them
It requires physical machines at the edge
questions.rationale: Functions-as-a-Service still executes on real servers; what is removed is the operator's job of provisioning, sizing and patching them. Billing is per invocation and per millisecond of execution.

questions.question: Designing across multiple availability zones primarily protects against:
options: The failure of a single data centre
questions.rationale: Availability zones are physically separate data centres within a region with independent power and networking; multi-zone designs survive one zone's outage. Surviving a whole region's loss needs multi-region design; code speed and passwords are unrelated concerns.

questions.question: Cloud migration of a long-running steady workload is most often optimised by:
options: Storing all data in the priciest region
questions.rationale: On-demand pricing is for spiky, unpredictable loads; steady workloads earn large discounts through 1-3 year reservations or committed-use plans - the core of FinOps cost optimisation. Monitoring cuts bills (it finds waste), never raises them.
